text: Yes. India's first dinosaur bones were found in Jabalpur in 1828. The word "dinosaur" was only invented in 1842.

In the [[@narmada|Narmada]] valley, scientists found hundreds of eggs laid by giant long-necked [[sauropod|sauropods]]. India also has footprints, [[fossil|fossil]] poo and bones from many kinds of dinosaur.
When most of these dinosaurs lived, India was an island, slowly drifting towards Asia. That makes its dinosaurs special. Some have close cousins in Madagascar and South America, but nowhere else.

sec.t:
The bones from Jabalpur were collected by William Henry Sleeman, a British army officer. Nobody knew what they were. Decades later, in 1877, the scientist Richard Lydekker named them Titanosaurus indicus, "titanic lizard of India". It was the first dinosaur named from India, and it gave its name to the whole group of titanosaurs.

Since then, Indian scientists have led most of the work. Teams from the Geological Survey of India, the Indian Statistical Institute, Panjab University and others have found new [[species|species]] in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Telangana and Tamil Nadu.

India's dinosaurs span most of the dinosaur age. Some of the oldest come from the Maleri rocks of Telangana, about 220 million years old, when dinosaurs were small and new. [[@barapasaurus|Barapasaurus]], one of the earliest big long-necks, lived by the Godavari about 190 million years ago.

In 2023, scientists named Tharosaurus from rocks near [[@india-wonder-jaisalmer|Jaisalmer]], about 167 million years old. It may be one of the oldest known members of the group that includes Diplodocus. At the very end of the age came [[@rajasaurus|Rajasaurus]], a horned meat-eater from Gujarat, and the great titanosaurs.

Long-necked titanosaurs were India's most common big dinosaurs near the end of the [[@dino-age-span|age of dinosaurs]]. Isisaurus, named after the Indian Statistical Institute, had unusually long front legs. Titanosaurs laid eggs in huge nesting grounds in Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh. Near Dhar, scientists found 92 nests holding 256 eggs.

Their [[@dino-eggs|eggs]] were about the size of a small football. At Dholi Dungri in Gujarat, a fossil snake was found coiled in a titanosaur nest, beside a hatchling.

Some of India's most important finds are not bones at all. At Pisdura in Maharashtra, [[@dino-poop|fossil dinosaur poo]] held tiny bits of grass, showing that grass grew in India while dinosaurs were alive. Near Jaisalmer in Rajasthan, three-toed [[@dino-feet-tracks|footprints]] are pressed into rock that was once a sandy shore. Each kind of clue fills in a different part of the picture.

{{story:india-drift}}

When these dinosaurs lived, India was drifting alone across the ocean, after breaking away from Madagascar about 88 million years ago. That's why its animals have cousins in Madagascar. Rajasaurus and Majungasaurus of Madagascar belong to the same family of short-armed hunters.

Near the end, India passed over a hot spot that fed the [[@deccan|Deccan eruptions]]. Many fossils lie in a layer of rock called the Lameta Formation, sandwiched just below the [[lava|lava]].

The Balasinor Dinosaur Fossil Park in Gujarat and the Dinosaur Fossil [[@national-parks|National Park]] in Dhar, Madhya Pradesh, protect places where fossils were found. Visitors can see eggs still in the rock. Some sites have suffered from people taking eggs and bones, which destroys clues forever. Protecting these sites, and keeping fossils in museums where scientists can study them, is now a big part of Indian palaeontology.

text: A tornado is a spinning column of air that reaches from a [[@thunderstorms|thunderstorm]] down to the ground. It starts when winds blow at different speeds and directions at different heights. The air between them begins to roll, like a pencil rolled between your hands.
A big thunderstorm's rising air can tip this rolling air upright. If it tightens and touches the ground, it becomes a tornado.

st.reveal: When wind near the ground and wind higher up blow differently, the air between them rolls like a rolling pin. A thunderstorm's rising air can tip that roll upright, into a spinning column.

Hold it upside down and swirl it quickly in circles for a few seconds, then stop. A spinning funnel forms inside, narrow at the bottom, just like the shape of a tornado.
myth: Opening windows during a tornado stops a house from exploding.

This old idea has been tested and rejected. Opening windows wastes precious time and lets in wind and flying debris. The safe thing is to get to a basement or a small room in the middle of the lowest floor, away from windows.

sec.t:
The most dangerous tornadoes come from giant, long-lasting thunderstorms called supercells. Inside them, the whole column of rising air slowly rotates. On weather radar, this rotation shows up as a hook shape at one corner of the storm.

As the spinning air stretches and narrows, it spins faster, the way a figure skater speeds up by pulling in their arms. Often a funnel of cloud drops from the base of the storm. Once the spinning reaches the ground, it's officially a tornado. Even so, most rotating storms never make one, and scientists are still working out why some do.

The central USA is perfect for tornadoes. Warm, wet air flows north from the Gulf of Mexico, while cold, dry air comes down from Canada and the [[@rocky-mountains|Rocky Mountains]]. When they crash together in spring, giant storms grow.

That stretch of flat land, from [[@texas|Texas]] up through Oklahoma and Kansas, is nicknamed Tornado Alley. No mountains stand in the way, so the air masses meet head-on. Many homes there have storm cellars, and schools practise tornado drills the way schools in Japan or Gujarat practise earthquake drills.

In the USA, the Storm Prediction Center in Norman, Oklahoma, watches for the right ingredients every day. When conditions look risky, it issues a tornado "watch". When radar shows rotation or someone spots a funnel, local forecasters issue a "warning", and sirens and phones go off. Better radar and [[@weather-forecasts|weather forecasts]] have given people precious minutes to take shelter.

Forecasters talk in chances, not certainties. A "30% chance of tornadoes" means that in many similar situations, about three in ten produce one nearby.

Tornadoes happen on every continent except Antarctica. Bangladesh, with its flat land and warm, wet air from the Bay of Bengal, gets some powerful ones. In 1989, a tornado near Dhaka was one of the deadliest ever recorded. India gets tornadoes now and then too, mostly in the east, and waterspouts sometimes spin over the sea.
A tornado is small, usually less than a kilometre wide, and lasts minutes. A [[@hurricanes|hurricane]] can be hundreds of kilometres wide and last for days.

text: Dolphins live in three kinds of places in India: big rivers, coastal [[lagoon|lagoons]] and the open sea. The most famous is the Ganges river dolphin, which lives in the Ganga, the Brahmaputra and their branches in states such as Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Assam and West Bengal.

India's first full count, published in 2025, found about 6,300 river dolphins. Almost all were Ganges river dolphins. Along the coast, Irrawaddy dolphins live in Chilika Lake in Odisha and in the Sundarbans. Out at sea, bottlenose, spinner and humpback dolphins swim off both coasts, and you can sometimes spot them from boats in Goa, Kerala and the Andaman Islands.

myth: Dolphins live only in the sea.

Several kinds of dolphin live in rivers. India has the Ganges river dolphin in the Ganga and Brahmaputra, and a tiny group of Indus river dolphins in Punjab's Beas river. Some dolphins, like the Irrawaddy dolphin, live in coastal lagoons and river mouths.

sec.t:
The Ganges river dolphin looks quite unlike the smiling sea dolphins in cartoons. It has a long, thin beak packed with sharp teeth, tiny eyes and a rounded forehead. Its eyes have no proper lens. It can tell light from dark, and not much more.

In muddy water, sight is not much use anyway. Instead, the dolphin sends out fast clicks and listens for the echoes bouncing back from fish and stones. This is called [[@echolocation|echolocation]]. It often swims on its side, sweeping its head and trailing a flipper along the riverbed, hunting for prawns and fish. It must come up to breathe every minute or two, and the sound of its breath, "susu", gave it its local name.

A close cousin, the Indus river dolphin, lives mainly in Pakistan. In India, a very small group survives in the Beas river in Punjab. The 2025 survey counted only three. Indus river dolphins were thought to have vanished from India decades ago, so their rediscovery in the Beas in 2007 was a pleasant shock. The stretch of river where they live is part of a protected [[wetland|wetland]], and Punjab's wildlife department now watches them closely.

The two river dolphins look almost the same. For a long time scientists thought they were one species. Studies of their skulls and [[gene|genes]] later showed they had been apart long enough to count as two.

[[@chilika|Chilika Lake]], a huge salty lagoon on the Odisha coast, is home to Irrawaddy dolphins. They have round heads with no beak, which makes them look a little like small whales. Recent counts put the number at about 150.

Boats take visitors out to watch them near the mouth of the lake, where it meets the Bay of Bengal. Too many noisy motorboats can disturb them, so local rules limit how close boats can go. Irrawaddy dolphins also live in the rivers and creeks of the [[@sundarbans-tigers|Sundarbans]], alongside crocodiles and tigers.

River dolphins face many dangers. Dams and barrages split rivers into pieces, so dolphin groups get cut off from one another. Some stretches dry up in summer as water is taken for farms and cities. Dolphins get tangled in fishing nets, and pollution from towns and factories harms the fish they eat.

In 2020 India launched Project Dolphin to protect both river and sea dolphins, and it now marks National Dolphin Day on 5 October. A second, wider count began in 2026. If the numbers hold steady, it will be good news for the rivers as well as the dolphins.

text: A [[wetland|wetland]] is land that is soaked with water for at least part of the year. Marshes, swamps, bogs, [[@mangroves|mangrove forests]], the edges of lakes and the flat land beside rivers all count.

Wetlands work like a giant sponge and a giant filter at the same time. They soak up floodwater and release it slowly. Their plants and mud trap dirt and break down pollution, so water leaves them cleaner than it came in. They are also nurseries: young fish, [[@frogs-world|frogs]], insects and birds grow up in their shallow, food-rich water. Freshwater wetlands cover only a small slice of the planet, yet a big share of all animal [[species|species]] depend on them.

st.reveal: Wetland soil and plants hold huge amounts of water and slow it down. The water seeps out over days or weeks instead of rushing into streets all at once. When wetlands are filled in and built over, floods often get worse.

sec.t:
Each winter, birds fly thousands of kilometres from Central Asia, Siberia and beyond to India's lakes and marshes. [[@chilika|Chilika Lake]] in Odisha, a huge salty [[lagoon|lagoon]] by the sea, can host around a million of them in a good year. Flocks of [[@flamingos-pink|flamingos]], ducks and waders feed in its shallows, and rare Irrawaddy dolphins swim in its channels. Fishing families in hundreds of villages around the lagoon depend on its prawns, crabs and fish.

Keoladeo National Park in Bharatpur, Rajasthan, began as a duck-hunting reserve for a maharaja. Today it is a protected bird [[sanctuary|sanctuary]] and a UNESCO [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage]] Site. It was once famous for Siberian cranes, but the last ones were seen there around 2002, after their numbers crashed along their long route.

In Florida, USA, [[@florida-everglades|the Everglades]] spread across a vast, slow-moving sheet of shallow water and sawgrass. In the early 1900s people dug canals to drain much of it for farms and towns. In 1947 the writer Marjory Stoneman Douglas published *The Everglades: River of Grass* and helped persuade Americans that the swamp was worth saving. The same year, part of it became a national park, and work to restore its water flow still goes on.

The Ramsar Convention, a world agreement to protect wetlands, was signed in 1971 in the town of Ramsar in Iran. India now has more than 100 Ramsar sites (103 in 2026), from [[@india-wonder-loktak|Loktak Lake]] in Manipur, with its floating islands of plants, to the mangroves of the [[@sundarbans-tigers|Sundarbans]].

Even so, about a third of the world's natural wetlands have vanished since 1970, faster than forests. Many were drained for farms or filled with rubbish and buildings. When a city loses its marshes, the [[monsoon|monsoon]] often answers with [[@floods-why|floods]] in places that never used to flood.

text: Wolves were wiped out of [[@usa-wonder-yellowstone|Yellowstone National Park]], in the western USA, by the 1920s. Without them, herds of elk grew large and stayed in the river valleys for long periods, nibbling young willow, aspen and cottonwood trees down to stubs.

In 1995 and 1996, park staff released 31 wolves caught in [[@canada|Canada]]. The wolves began hunting elk, and elk numbers fell. Some researchers found that willows and aspens then began to grow back along certain streams. Their roots helped hold riverbanks in place, and beavers returned to build dams. That chain of events, from a [[predator|predator]] at the top down to the shape of a stream, is called a *trophic cascade*. How strong it really was in Yellowstone is still argued about.

st.reveal: Elk numbers in the northern part of the park dropped a lot over the next twenty years, and elk spent less time in some open river valleys. Wolves were one cause. Hunting outside the park, bears, cougars and dry years also played a part.

sec.t:
The first wolves were carried into the park in metal crates in January 1995. They were kept in large fenced pens to settle in, then set free. Within a few years they formed packs and spread across the park.

Ecologists William Ripple and Robert Beschta studied willow and aspen along streams. They reported that some trees, nibbled to the ground for decades, began shooting upward. Beaver colonies on the park's northern range grew from one in 1996 to about nine by 2009. Ponds behind beaver dams gave homes to fish, frogs and birds. In 2014 a short [[@youtube|online video]] called "How Wolves Change Rivers" told this story and was watched by millions.

Other researchers looked at the same park and saw a more mixed picture. Elk numbers were also cut by human hunters outside the park, by a growing number of bears and cougars, and by harsh winters and dry summers. In many spots willows stayed short.

Some streams had changed so much while the wolves were gone that a few more trees could not fix them. Without beavers to raise the water level, banks had cut deep, and willow roots could no longer reach the water. Later studies that measured many more trees across the park found smaller effects than the early reports. Most scientists now agree that wolves matter, but they are one part of a complicated system, not a magic switch.

The idea that big predators help keep whole landscapes healthy has spread around the world. In India, protecting tigers in reserves like Kanha and Corbett also protects the forests, rivers and smaller animals that share their home. That is one reason the [[@tiger-stripes|tiger]] is called an "umbrella" [[species|species]].

Today, Yellowstone usually holds around a hundred wolves in about ten packs. Visitors with telescopes gather in the Lamar Valley at dawn to watch them. Wolves that wander outside the park, though, can still be legally hunted in some neighbouring states, and the arguments that began in 1995 have never fully ended.

text: A soap bubble is a ball of air wrapped in a very thin skin of water held between two layers of soap. When light hits that skin, some of it bounces off the outer surface and some bounces off the inner surface.

These two reflections travel slightly different distances. When they meet again, some colours line up and get brighter, while others cancel each other out. Which colours win depends on how thick the film is at that exact spot. Since the thickness keeps changing, the colours swirl and shift.

Scientists call this thin-film [[interference|interference]]. It needs a film whose thickness is close to the size of a light wave, which is why a bubble shows colours and a glass of soapy water does not.

st.reveal: Gravity pulls the soapy water down, so the top of the film thins out first. As the thickness changes, so does the colour. Soon a dark patch appears at the top, which means the film is about to break.

sec.t:
Light travels as waves, and each colour has its own [[wavelength|wavelength]]. Red waves are the longest that our eyes can see, at about 700 nanometres. Violet waves are shortest, at about 400. A nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre.

A bubble's skin is often only a few hundred nanometres thick. That is hundreds of times thinner than a hair on your head. It is also just about the same size as the light waves landing on it.

When the light reflected from the back of the film comes out exactly in step with the light from the front, that colour looks bright. When the two come out of step, the peaks of one wave fill the dips of the other and that colour fades away. Change the thickness by a tiny amount and a different colour comes out in step.

{{story:peacock-tail}}

sec.h: A bubble that is always draining
sec.t:
A bubble is never still. [[gravity|Gravity]] pulls the water in the film downwards, so the bottom grows thicker while the top grows thinner. Water also evaporates into the air. Puffs of air swirl the film around, which is why the colours seem to flow like [[@crayons-paints|oil paint]].

Sugar or glycerine in bubble mix slows the drying, so bubbles last longer and the colours have more time to play. The soap itself matters too. It lowers the water's [[surface-tension|surface tension]] and keeps the skin stretchy instead of letting it snap. That stretchiness is also why bubbles pull themselves into [[@bubbles-round|spheres]].

Watch a bubble long enough and you may see a dark patch near the top. The film there has become thinner than about 30 nanometres. At that thickness, the two reflections cancel almost every colour we can see, so very little light comes back to your eye. The patch looks black against the shining colours around it.

A black patch is a warning. The film is close to its limit, and the bubble usually pops within seconds.

More than 300 years ago, Isaac Newton spent hours watching soap bubbles. In his book Opticks, published in 1704, he described how the colours appear in rings and bands and change in a fixed order as the film thins. He measured the patterns carefully, even though nobody yet understood light as waves. [[@newton-life|Newton]] thought light was a stream of tiny particles, and later scientists used the wave idea to explain what he had seen.

The same effect paints the swirl of colours on a puddle with a little oil on it, after rain on a city road. A peacock's [[@peacock-tail|shimmering tail]] uses a related trick, with layers built into its feathers instead of a film of soap. A [[@rainbow-how|rainbow]] is different, because raindrops bend light rather than bouncing it between two surfaces.

text: A solar cooker catches sunlight and turns it into heat for cooking. The most common kind, a box cooker, is an insulated box painted black inside, with a glass or clear plastic lid and often a mirror on a hinged flap.

Sunlight passes through the glass and hits the black inside and the dark pots. Dark surfaces soak up light and get hot. That heat then has trouble escaping. The glass lid stops warm air from drifting away, and the insulation keeps the walls from losing heat. The mirror bounces extra sunlight in.
Inside, temperatures often reach about 90 to 150 °C. That's enough to boil water, cook rice and dal, or bake a cake, though more slowly than on a stove.

st.prompt: You put two identical pots of water in a solar box cooker, one painted black and one shiny silver. Which gets hottest?
st.reveal: Black surfaces soak up most of the light that hits them and turn it into heat. Shiny surfaces reflect light away. That's why solar cookers use black pots inside and shiny reflectors outside, to bounce extra sunlight onto them.

sec.t:
You've felt this effect in a car parked in the sun with its windows closed. Light streams in through the glass and warms the seats. The warm air can't get out, so the car becomes much hotter than the air outside.

A solar box cooker does the same on purpose. Colour matters a lot. A black pot soaks up most of the light that hits it, while a shiny or white pot reflects much of it away. Lids on the pots help too, keeping steam and heat inside. The [[@sun-what|Sun]] sends a surprising amount of energy. On a clear day, each square metre of ground in sunlight receives roughly 1,000 watts, about as much as a small electric heater.

In the 1760s, a Swiss scientist named Horace-Bénédict de Saussure built a box with layers of glass on top and a black base. He found it got hot enough to cook fruit. Later scientists used similar boxes on [[expedition|expeditions]]. India has had solar cooker programmes since the 1980s, and the government has long supported cheap box cookers for homes.

Some of India's largest kitchens now use sunlight on a giant scale. Two examples are the Brahma Kumaris centre at Mount Abu in Rajasthan and the Sai Baba temple at Shirdi in Maharashtra. There, rows of large curved mirrors on the roof focus sunlight to make steam. The steam cooks food for thousands of people a day.

Around the world, a very large number of people still cook over wood, dung or charcoal fires. Smoke from these fires fills homes and harms people's lungs, and it is a major cause of indoor [[@air-pollution|air pollution]]. Collecting firewood takes hours and cuts down trees.

Solar cookers can help, though they have limits. They need clear skies and daytime cooking, they're slow, and they don't suit every dish or every family. In high, sunny places like [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], where firewood is scarce and the sun is strong even in winter, they have been especially useful. Many families use a solar cooker alongside a regular stove, cooking a pot of [[@pulses-dal|dal]] in the sun while saving fuel for the evening meal.

sec.t:
तेल्ला पोनिकी गाँव के आसपास की पहाड़ियों पर उगता है। कारीगर इसे काटते हैं, सूखने देते हैं और फिर हर हिस्से को अलग-अलग गढ़ते हैं। यहाँ एक धड़, वहाँ एक सूँड, कतार में चार पैर। हिस्से तैयार होने पर उन्हें *मक्कु* से जोड़ा जाता है, जो पिसे इमली के बीज और लकड़ी के बुरादे से बना लेप है।

फिर आती है घिसाई, खड़िया जैसी एक परत, और रंगाई। पुराने खिलौनों में पौधों और [[mineral|खनिजों]] से बने रंग लगते थे। आज बहुत-से खिलौनों पर चमकदार इनेमल पेंट लगता है। तैयार खिलौने इतने हल्के होते हैं कि कोई बच्चा पूरा हाथी एक हथेली पर उठा ले। एक को पानी भरी बाल्टी में डालो, तो वह कॉर्क की तरह ऊपर-नीचे डोलता रहेगा।

त्योहारों पर कोंडापल्ली खिलौने जी उठते हैं। संक्रांति और दशहरे पर आंध्र प्रदेश, तेलंगाना और तमिलनाडु के बहुत-से परिवार *बोम्मला कोलुवु* सजाते हैं, यानी लकड़ी की सीढ़ियों पर गुड़ियों की सजावट। सबसे ऊपर की सीढ़ियों पर देवता बैठते हैं, फिर राजा और संत, और नीचे आम लोग और जानवर।

पड़ोसी एक-दूसरे की सीढ़ियाँ देखने आते हैं, बच्चे गाते हैं और कोई मिठाई बाँटता है। कुछ परिवार वही गुड़ियाएँ 50 साल या उससे भी ज़्यादा सँभालकर रखते हैं और हर साल एक नई जोड़ते हैं, इसलिए सजावट परिवार के साथ-साथ बढ़ती जाती है।

बहुत-से परिवार गुड़ियों को विषम संख्या की सीढ़ियों पर सजाने का पुराना [[ritual|रिवाज]] मानते हैं, अक्सर तीन, पाँच, सात या नौ। कोंडापल्ली के सेट इसी के लिए बनते हैं। पूरा दशावतार सेट विष्णु के दसों रूप एक कतार में दिखाता है, मछली से लेकर योद्धा राजा तक, हर एक पेंसिल जितना ऊँचा। लकड़ी इतनी हल्की है कि देवताओं की भीड़ के नीचे ऊँची सीढ़ियाँ भी नहीं झुकतीं।

कोंडापल्ली के बहुत-से कारीगर आर्यक्षत्रिय कहलाने वाले समुदाय से हैं। परिवारों के किस्से कहते हैं कि उनके [[ancestor|पूर्वज]] कई सौ साल पहले राजस्थान से आए, शायद विजयनगर के महान राजाओं के ज़माने में। इतिहासकार इसे मुमकिन मानते हैं, क्योंकि कुछ डिज़ाइनों में राजस्थानी कला की झलक है, पर अब तक कोई लिखित रिकॉर्ड नहीं मिला जो बात पक्की कर दे।

आज यह कला मुश्किल में है। प्लास्टिक के सस्ते खिलौने कम दाम में मिलते हैं, और खास पेड़ मिलना कठिन होता जा रहा है। कुछ परिवार नक्काशी छोड़कर दूसरे कामों में चले गए हैं। कुछ अब बड़े खिलौनों के साथ चाबी के छल्ले और फ़्रिज मैग्नेट भी बनाते हैं, और अमेरिका और यूरोप के खरीदारों को ऑनलाइन बेचते हैं।

कोंडापल्ली भारत का अकेला खिलौना गाँव नहीं है। लगभग 650 किलोमीटर दूर कर्नाटक में [[@channapatna-toys|चन्नपटना]] के लाख वाले लकड़ी के खिलौने तेज़ घूमती खराद पर बनते हैं। उनके कारीगर तेज़ी से घूमती लकड़ी पर सख़्त लाख की डंडी दबाकर रंग चढ़ाते हैं, और [[friction|घर्षण]] की गर्मी से रंग पिघलकर लकड़ी पर चढ़ जाता है।

text: ऑपेरा एक ऐसा नाटक है जिसमें कहानी बोली नहीं, गाई जाती है, और साथ में ऑर्केस्ट्रा बजता है। इसमें गायन, अभिनय, संगीत, वेशभूषा और मंच-सज्जा, सब कुछ अक्सर बड़े पैमाने पर मिला होता है। ऑपेरा की शुरुआत लगभग 1600 में इटली में हुई, और वहाँ से यह पूरे यूरोप और फिर दुनिया भर में फैल गया।

ऑपेरा गायक अपनी ज़बरदस्त, बिना माइक वाली आवाज़ों के लिए मशहूर हैं। वे सालों तक ताकत और काबू के साथ गाने की तालीम लेते हैं, ताकि बड़े हॉलों में बिना [[@microphones|माइक्रोफ़ोन]] के पूरे [[@orchestra|ऑर्केस्ट्रा]] के ऊपर सुनाई दे सकें। कुछ ऑपेरा हास्य होते हैं, कुछ दुखांत, और कुछ [[@fairy-tales|परीकथाएँ]] या पौराणिक कहानियाँ। 'ऑपेरा' शब्द का इतालवी में बस इतना मतलब है, 'काम' या 'रचना'।

sec.t:
ज़्यादातर ऑपेरा दो तरह के गायन के बीच आते-जाते रहते हैं। रेचितातीव में किरदार तेज़ी से, लगभग बोलचाल की तरह गाते हैं, ताकि कहानी आगे बढ़े। आरिया में कहानी थम जाती है और कोई किरदार अपनी भावनाओं पर एक लंबा, सुंदर गीत गाता है। आरिया ही वे हिस्से हैं जो दर्शकों को याद रहते हैं और जिन्हें वे घर लौटते हुए गुनगुनाते हैं।

गायकों को इस हिसाब से बाँटा जाता है कि उनकी आवाज़ कितनी ऊँची जाती है। सबसे ऊँची से सबसे नीची तक, इनमें सोप्रानो, मेज़ो-सोप्रानो, टेनर, बैरिटोन और बेस हैं। नायिकाएँ अक्सर सोप्रानो होती हैं, नायक टेनर, और खलनायक या बूढ़े राजा बेस।

बहुत-से सबसे मशहूर ऑपेरा 1700 और 1800 के दशकों के हैं। [[@mozart|मोत्ज़ार्ट]] ने *द मैजिक फ़्लूट* और *द मैरिज ऑफ़ फ़िगारो* लिखे। इटली के जुसेप्पे वेर्दी ने प्राचीन मिस्र में रची कहानी *आइदा* लिखी। जर्मनी के रिचर्ड वागनर ने *द रिंग ऑफ़ द निबेलुंग* लिखा, यानी चार जुड़े हुए ऑपेरा, जिन्हें कई शामों में खेलने में लगभग 15 घंटे लगते हैं। सोचो, लगभग पाँच लंबी फ़िल्मों जितना।

जियाकोमो पुच्चीनी के *मादामा बटरफ़्लाई* और *ला बोहेम* आज भी ऑपेरा हाउसों को भर देते हैं। न्यूयॉर्क में 1883 में बना मेट्रोपॉलिटन ऑपेरा दुनिया की सबसे बड़ी ऑपेरा कंपनियों में से एक है।

sec.t: ऑपेरा गायक की ताकत चिल्लाने से नहीं, तालीम से आती है। गायक [[diaphragm|डायाफ़्राम]] का इस्तेमाल करते हुए पेट से गहरी साँस लेते हैं, और गले को खुला और ढीला रखते हैं। वे ऊँची [[frequency|आवृत्तियों]] की एक पट्टी को, लगभग 3,000 [[vibration|कंपन]] प्रति सेकंड के आसपास, उभारना सीखते हैं, जिसे ऑर्केस्ट्रा ज़्यादा नहीं ढकता। यही खनक [[@voice|आवाज़]] को संगीत चीरकर आखिरी कतार तक पहुँचा देती है।

यूरोप के कई ऑपेरा भारत में रचे गए हैं, हालाँकि अक्सर कल्पना भरे ढंग से। लेओ देलीब का *लाक्मे* (1883) ब्रिटिश भारत में घटता है, और इसका 'फ़्लावर डुएट' आज दुनिया भर की फ़िल्मों और विज्ञापनों में सुनाई देता है।

1980 में अमेरिकी संगीतकार फ़िलिप ग्लास ने *सत्याग्रह* लिखा, जो [[@gandhi-south-africa|दक्षिण अफ़्रीका में गांधी जी के सालों]] के बारे में है। इसके बोल भगवद्गीता से लिए गए हैं और संस्कृत में गाए जाते हैं। यह न्यूयॉर्क के मेट्रोपॉलिटन ऑपेरा में भी खेला जा चुका है। भारत की संगीत-नाटक की अपनी परंपराएँ भी हैं, संस्कृत रंगमंच से लेकर पारसी थिएटर और गाँव की प्रस्तुतियों तक, जो कुछ इसी तरह गीतों से कहानियाँ कहती हैं।

text: A tessellation is a pattern of shapes that covers a flat surface with no gaps and no overlaps, like tiles on a bathroom floor.

Only three regular shapes can do it alone: equal-sided triangles, squares and hexagons. The reason is in their corners. Where tiles meet at a point, their angles must add up to a full turn of 360 degrees. Six triangle corners of 60 degrees do that. So do four square corners of 90 degrees, and three hexagon corners of 120 degrees.
A regular pentagon has corners of 108 degrees. Three of them make 324, leaving a gap. Four make 432, which is too many. So regular pentagons never fit.

Mix shapes and more patterns appear. Squares and octagons together make a common floor pattern, with a small square filling each gap between four octagons. Two octagon corners of 135 degrees and one square corner of 90 add up to exactly 360.

st.prompt: Which of these regular shapes can cover a floor with no gaps on its own?
st.reveal: Each corner of a regular hexagon is 120 degrees, and three of them meet at a point to make exactly 360. A pentagon's corners are 108 degrees, which doesn't divide 360 evenly, so gaps appear.

sec.t:
Lopsided pentagons are a different story. Some of them do tile, and for about a hundred years mathematicians tried to find every kind.

In 1975, the American writer Martin Gardner described the hunt in a magazine column. A reader named Marjorie Rice, a homemaker in San Diego with no maths training beyond high school, began drawing in her kitchen. Over the next few years she discovered four new kinds that the experts had missed.

In 2015, three researchers at the University of Washington Bothell used a computer search to find a fifteenth kind. Two years later, a French mathematician, Michaël Rao, used a computer to show that the list was finally complete. There are exactly 15.

People have been making tessellations for thousands of years. Islamic artists built some of the most complicated ones, using stars and polygons in tiles and carved stone. You can see them at the [[@spain|Alhambra]] palace in Spain, and in the stone screens and inlay of Mughal buildings such as the [[@taj-mahal|Taj Mahal]].

In the 1930s, a Dutch artist named [[@maths-art|M.C. Escher]] visited the [[@alhambra|Alhambra]] and came home inspired. He began drawing tessellations of birds, fish and lizards that lock together perfectly.

Mathematicians later showed there are exactly 17 basic ways to repeat a pattern across a flat surface, each with its own [[@symmetry|symmetry]]. Artists in many places had already found most of them by eye.

Bees build their combs from hexagons. Of the three regular shapes that tile, the [[@honeycomb|hexagon]] uses the least wall to hold the most space, which saves wax.

The same shape turns up where cooling [[lava|lava]] cracks into tall columns, or where mud dries out and splits into a pattern of plates. At the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland, about 40,000 stone columns pack tightly together, many of them six-sided. In each case, the cracks or walls meet at corners that close up with no gaps, the same rule that decides which tiles fit on your floor.

text: हमारा शरीर लगभग 37°C पर सबसे अच्छा काम करता है। बहुत गर्म दिन में उसे इसी तापमान पर टिके रहने के लिए खूब मेहनत करनी पड़ती है। त्वचा के पास की खून की नलियाँ चौड़ी हो जाती हैं, ताकि ज़्यादा गर्म खून हवा को अपनी गर्मी दे सके। इसीलिए चेहरा लाल हो जाता है। और फिर पसीना आता है। पसीना त्वचा से [[evaporation|भाप बनकर उड़ता]] है, तो अपने साथ गर्मी भी ले जाता है।

अगर पसीने में बहुत ज़्यादा पानी निकल जाए और तुम पूरा पानी न पियो, तो शरीर में पानी की कमी हो जाती है। थकान, चक्कर और सिरदर्द होने लगता है। और अगर शरीर खुद को बिल्कुल ठंडा न कर पाए, तो अंदर का तापमान ख़तरनाक हद तक चढ़ सकता है। इसे लू लगना या हीटस्ट्रोक कहते हैं, और यह मेडिकल इमरजेंसी है।

sec.t:
दिमाग के भीतर हाइपोथैलेमस नाम का एक छोटा हिस्सा थर्मोस्टैट की तरह काम करता है। जैसे ही उसे लगता है कि खून ज़्यादा गर्म हो रहा है, वह ठंडक का बटन दबा देता है। दिल तेज़ी से पंप करने लगता है, ताकि ज़्यादा खून त्वचा तक पहुँचे। लाखों [[@sweat|पसीने]] की [[gland|ग्रंथियाँ]] नमकीन पानी छोड़ने लगती हैं।

पसीना बहाने में इंसान कमाल के हैं। ज़्यादातर [[mammal|स्तनधारियों]] के मुकाबले हमारे पास पसीने की ग्रंथियाँ ज़्यादा हैं, और शरीर पर बाल बहुत कम। कई वैज्ञानिक मानते हैं कि इसी वजह से हमारे [[ancestor|पूर्वज]] अफ़्रीका की तपती दोपहर में भी शिकार कर पाते थे और लंबी दूरी तय कर लेते थे, जब बाकी जानवरों को छाँव में आराम करना पड़ता था।

sec.h: उमस वाली गर्मी ज़्यादा क्यों सताती है

sec.t:
पहले आती है गर्मी से थकावट। इसके [[symptom|लक्षण]] हैं खूब पसीना, कमज़ोरी, सिरदर्द, जी मिचलाना और ऐंठन। किसी ठंडी जगह जाकर आराम करने और घूँट-घूँट पानी पीने से आम तौर पर आराम मिल जाता है।

लू लगना इससे कहीं गंभीर है। शरीर का तापमान 40°C या उससे ऊपर जा सकता है, त्वचा छूने पर गर्म लग सकती है, और इंसान उलझन में पड़ सकता है या बेहोश हो सकता है। उसे तुरंत डॉक्टरी मदद चाहिए। तब तक बड़े लोग उसे छाँव में ले जाकर पानी और पंखे से ठंडा कर सकते हैं। छोटे बच्चे, बुज़ुर्ग, धूप में काम करने वाले लोग और कुछ बीमारियों वाले लोग सबसे ज़्यादा ख़तरे में होते हैं। इसीलिए [[@heatwaves|लू के दिनों]] में पड़ोसियों का हालचाल लेते रहना ज़रूरी है।

sec.h: भारत और अमेरिका की रिकॉर्ड गर्मी
sec.t:
भारत का अब तक का सबसे ऊँचा तापमान 51.0°C है, जो 19 मई 2016 को राजस्थान के फलोदी में मापा गया। उत्तर भारत के कई शहरों में मई-जून में पारा अक्सर 45°C के पार चला जाता है। भारतीय मौसम विज्ञान विभाग लू की चेतावनी जारी करता है, और कई शहरों के पास अब गर्मी से निपटने की कार्य-योजना है। 2010 की जानलेवा लू के बाद, 2013 में अहमदाबाद दक्षिण एशिया के पहले शहरों में था जिसने ऐसी योजना बनाई। इसमें मोबाइल पर एसएमएस से चेतावनी, ठंडे आश्रय, और कुछ छतों को सफ़ेद रंगना शामिल है ताकि धूप लौट जाए।

अमेरिका में कैलिफ़ोर्निया की डेथ वैली के नाम 1913 का 56.7°C वाला आधिकारिक विश्व रिकॉर्ड है, हालाँकि कुछ जलवायु वैज्ञानिक उस पुरानी माप पर सवाल उठाते हैं। जुलाई 2023 में एरिज़ोना के फ़ीनिक्स शहर में लगातार 31 दिन पारा 110°F (लगभग 43°C) या उससे ऊपर रहा।

सबसे सीधी सलाह ही सबसे कारगर है। प्यास लगने से पहले भी थोड़ी-थोड़ी देर में [[@water-drink|पानी]] पीते रहो। ढीले, हल्के रंग के सूती कपड़े पहनो और सिर पर टोपी रखो। सबसे गर्म घंटों में, आम तौर पर दोपहर 12 से 4 बजे तक, छाँव में रहो। दादी-नानी के नुस्खे भी काम आते हैं: छाछ, चुटकी भर नमक वाला नींबू-पानी, और मटके का पानी, जो [[@evaporation-cooling|भाप बनने]] से ठंडा रहता है।

जानवरों के अपने तरीके हैं। कुत्ते जीभ निकालकर हाँफते हैं, हाथी अपने बड़े-बड़े कान फड़फड़ाते हैं, और रेगिस्तान के कई जीव दिन भर सोते रहते हैं और रात को बाहर निकलते हैं।

text: It depends on two numbers: how much energy the battery holds, and how much power the charger delivers. Battery size is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh). Charger power is measured in kilowatts (kW). Divide one by the other and you get the time.

Take a small electric car with a 40 kWh battery, a common size for Indian city cars. From an ordinary home socket giving about 3 kW, it takes roughly 13 hours to charge from empty. A 7 kW wall box does it in about 6 hours. A highway fast charger can take it from 10% to 80% in around half an hour.

st.reveal: Divide energy by power, 40 ÷ 7, and you get just under 6 hours. In real life it takes a little longer, because some energy is lost as heat and charging slows near the top.

sec.t:
Time = energy ÷ power. That's it. A 60 kWh battery on a 7 kW wall box takes about 60 ÷ 7, or 8 to 9 hours. On a 150 kW fast charger it would, in theory, take 60 ÷ 150, or 24 minutes.

In real life, add a bit. Some energy turns to heat in the cables and the battery, perhaps 10% at home. And a battery can't take full power all the way. It works a bit like filling a bucket at a tap: easy at first, then you slow down near the brim so it doesn't spill. The idea is the same as working out [[@speed-distance|speed, distance and time]], just with energy instead of kilometres.

A lithium-ion battery can swallow energy quickly when it's fairly empty. As it fills, pushing more in creates heat and stress, which would wear the battery out sooner. So the car's computer slows things down, often sharply after about 80%.

That's why charging times are usually quoted from 10% to 80%. The last 20% can take almost as long as the first 70%. On a long drive, it's often quicker to stop twice for a short top-up than once for a full charge. The same chemistry is at work in a [[@batteries-phones|phone battery]], which also slows down near full.

In India, most electric vehicles aren't cars at all. They are scooters, motorbikes and e-rickshaws. A scooter battery is small, often 2 to 4 kWh, so it can charge from a normal socket in a few hours.

Some companies skip charging altogether. At a battery-swapping station, a rider pulls out an empty battery and slots in a full one in a couple of minutes, much like buying a new gas cylinder. This works well for delivery riders and autorickshaw drivers, who can't afford to wait.

sec.h: Cleaner, if the power is clean
sec.t: An electric car makes no exhaust, but its electricity has to come from somewhere. If that's coal, some pollution has simply moved to a power station. As countries add more [[@renewable-energy|solar and wind power]], charging gets cleaner. Many drivers now charge at midday when solar power is cheap, or overnight when demand is low, letting the car's battery soak up spare electricity that would otherwise go to waste.

text: Most inventions fail. Some don't work. But many that work fine still flop, because people don't want them, can't afford them or aren't ready for them yet.

A product has to solve a real problem, at a price people will pay, at a moment when they are ready to change their habits. Miss any one of those and even a clever machine ends up in a cupboard. The good news is that failure often teaches inventors what to try next. Some of the most common things you use today grew out of ideas that flopped first.

options.t: VHS tapes could record for longer, enough for a whole film

st.reveal: Many people thought Betamax had a slightly better picture. But early VHS tapes could record about two hours, long enough for a film or a match, while early Betamax tapes held about one. More companies made VHS machines, and shops stocked more VHS films.

Smithsonian Institution, National Museum of American History, AT&T Picturephone.
Britannica, Betamax and VHS.

d.try: Invent something useful from a cardboard box, string and tape. Before you build, write down who would use it and what problem it solves. Then let three people test it and note what goes wrong. Change one thing and test again, the way real inventors do.
myth: A good invention always succeeds if it works well.

Plenty of inventions that worked perfectly still failed. They cost too much, came too early, solved a problem nobody had or clashed with how people wanted to live. Success depends on people as much as on machines.
facts: Picturephone shown at New York World's Fair
79 days in 1985 before the old recipe returned

sec.t:
In 1964, at the World's Fair in New York, the American phone company AT&T showed off the Picturephone. You could see the person you were talking to on a small screen. People loved the demo. But it was costly, the screen was tiny, and very few people had one, so there was nobody to call. It faded away.

Fifty years later, [[@tech-video-calls|video calls]] on phones became everyday life. The idea was right. The timing, the price and the networks were wrong. [[@electric-cars|Electric cars]] had a similar story. They were common in American cities around 1900, then lost out to cheap petrol cars for most of a century.

sec.h: When people don't like the feel of it
sec.t:
Some products bump into feelings. In 1985, Coca-Cola changed its famous recipe. Taste tests had said people liked the new flavour, but many customers were furious about losing the old one. After 79 days, the original came back.

Google Glass, smart glasses with a tiny screen and camera, went on sale to early users in 2013. Many people felt uneasy being near someone who might be filming them. Shoppers didn't take to it, and Google later stopped selling it to the public.

In 1985 in Britain, inventor Clive Sinclair launched the C5, a small electric tricycle. It was low to the ground, slow and open to rain, and drivers felt unsafe next to lorries. Only a few thousand were sold.

In India, the Tata Nano was unveiled in 2008 as the world's cheapest car, at about one lakh rupees. It was meant to move families off risky scooters. But many buyers didn't want to be seen in "the cheapest car", and sales stayed far below plans. Production ended in 2018.

In 1968, a scientist at the company 3M made a glue that stuck only lightly and peeled off easily. Nobody knew what to do with it. Years later, a colleague used it to keep bookmarks in his hymn book from falling out, and [[@accident-post-it|Post-it notes]] were born.

Thomas Edison and his team tested thousands of materials before finding a long-lasting [[@light-bulb|light bulb]] filament. A museum in Sweden, the Museum of Failure, now displays flops so people can learn from them. And the strangest part? Most inventions protected by [[@patents|patents]], the legal rules that guard new ideas, never earn their inventors any money at all.

text: When British India was divided in 1947, Pakistan was made from two Muslim-majority regions far apart: West Pakistan, and East Pakistan, which was Bengal's eastern half. More people lived in the East, but power, money and the army were mostly in the West.

After years of unfair treatment, East Pakistan's people demanded self-rule. In March 1971 the army cracked down, and Bengali leaders declared independence. Nine months of fighting followed. In December, India entered the war. On 16 December, Pakistan's forces in the East surrendered, and Bangladesh became a free country.

st.prompt: Before 1971, what was the land of Bangladesh called?
st.reveal: From 1947, Pakistan had two parts, East and West, far apart on either side of India. East Pakistan became Bangladesh in 1971. West Bengal is the neighbouring Indian state.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Bangladesh Liberation War and Indo-Pakistani War of 1971.
UNHCR, The State of the World's Refugees 2000, chapter on the 1971 crisis in South Asia.
n.certNote: The main events are well documented. The number of people killed in 1971 is strongly disputed, with estimates ranging from a few hundred thousand to 3 million, and historians in different countries tell parts of the story differently.

d.try: On a map of South Asia, find Karachi and Dhaka. Use the scale bar and a piece of string to measure the distance between them. Then think about how hard it would be to run one country from two pieces that far apart.
myth: India created Bangladesh in a two-week war.

The fight for Bangladesh began in March 1971, led by Bengalis themselves, including the Mukti Bahini freedom fighters. India's army joined in December and the war ended quickly, but the struggle had gone on for nine months.
facts: 16 December, marked in Bangladesh and as Vijay Diwas in India

sec.t:
At [[@partition|Partition]], the new Pakistan had two wings with about 1,600 km of India between them. They shared a religion, but not much else. The people of the East spoke Bengali, ate rice and fish, and had their own literature and music. Most leaders in the West spoke Urdu or Punjabi.

In 1948, the government declared that Urdu alone would be the national language. Students in Dhaka protested. On 21 February 1952, police fired on a protest and several students died. Bangladesh remembers them every year, and UNESCO later made 21 February International Mother Language Day, which is why the [[@bengali-language|Bengali language]] holds a special place in the story.

In November 1970, a terrible [[cyclone|cyclone]] hit East Pakistan and killed hundreds of thousands of people. Many felt the government in the West was slow to help.

A month later, Pakistan held a national election. The Awami League, led by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, won almost every seat in the East, enough for a majority in the whole [[parliament|parliament]]. But the leaders in the West would not hand over power. Talks failed.

On the night of 25 March 1971, the Pakistani army began a crackdown in Dhaka. Students, teachers and ordinary people were killed. Bengali leaders declared independence the next day.

{{story:refugees}}

Bengali soldiers, students and villagers formed the Mukti Bahini, the "freedom force", and fought a guerrilla war. Many terrible things happened that year, and people in Bangladesh remember them as a genocide. How many died is still argued over.

About 10 million [[@refugees|refugees]] crossed into India, mostly into West Bengal, Tripura and Assam. It was one of the biggest [[refugee|refugee]] movements of the 20th century. India housed and fed them in camps, at a huge cost. Prime Minister [[@indira-gandhi|Indira Gandhi]] travelled abroad to ask other countries for help, with mixed success.

On 3 December 1971, Pakistan's air force struck Indian airfields. India declared war. Indian forces and the Mukti Bahini moved fast towards Dhaka, while India's navy blocked the ports.

The war pulled in the big powers of the [[@cold-war|Cold War]]. India had signed a friendship [[treaty|treaty]] with the Soviet Union that August. The United States backed Pakistan and sent a group of warships, led by the [[@aircraft-carriers|aircraft carrier]] USS *Enterprise*, into the Bay of Bengal. By the time it arrived, the fighting was nearly over.

The war lasted 13 days. On 16 December, Lieutenant General A. A. K. Niazi of Pakistan signed the surrender in Dhaka before Lieutenant General Jagjit Singh Aurora of India. About 93,000 soldiers and officials became prisoners of war. Most were returned to Pakistan after the Simla Agreement of 1972 between India and Pakistan.

Sheikh Mujibur Rahman returned home in January 1972 and became Bangladesh's leader. The country began with a ruined [[economy|economy]] and millions of people coming back to burned villages. Bengali became the official language.

Bangladesh has changed a great deal since then. Today it has about 17 crore people (2024) and is one of the biggest makers of clothes in the world. Its people still mark 16 December as Victory Day, and 26 March as Independence Day.

text: Mansa Musa was a king of the Mali Empire, which stretched across West Africa in the 1300s. "Mansa" means king or emperor. He ruled from about 1312 to 1337, when Mali controlled some of the richest gold fields in the world.

He is famous above all for one journey. In 1324 he set off on the Hajj, the Muslim [[pilgrimage|pilgrimage]] to Mecca, crossing the [[@sahara|Sahara]] with a vast [[caravan|caravan]]. Writers in Cairo were still talking about it years later. He spent and gave away so much gold that its value dropped there. He came home with scholars and builders and turned the city of Timbuktu into a centre of learning.

st.prompt: Besides gold, which everyday thing was so valuable in Mali that traders swapped slabs of it like money?
st.reveal: Salt was dug from mines deep in the Sahara and carried south on camels. People living in hot lands need salt to stay healthy, and there was little of it near Mali's gold fields.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Musa I of Mali.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Timbuktu.
Nehemia Levtzion, Ancient Ghana and Mali (1973).
n.certNote: The main events of Mansa Musa's life are well recorded by writers of his time. The exact size of his caravan and his wealth are not, and modern figures for his "net worth" are guesses.

d.try: On a world map or a globe, find Timbuktu in Mali, then Cairo in Egypt, then Mecca. Lay a piece of string along the route and use the map's scale to measure it. In a straight line it is roughly 5,000 km, and Mansa Musa's caravan walked farther than that, much of it through desert.
myth: Mansa Musa was the richest person who ever lived, worth hundreds of billions of dollars.

He was certainly enormously rich, but there is no fair way to compare his wealth with modern billionaires. The big dollar numbers you see online are modern estimates without real evidence behind them.
facts: the Djinguereber Mosque, Timbuktu, begun around 1327
gold, salt and trade across the Sahara

sec.t:
Mali grew rich by standing between two things people wanted. To the south lay gold fields, where miners dug and panned for gold. To the north, deep in the Sahara, lay salt mines at places like Taghaza, where people cut salt into heavy slabs.

People in hot lands lose salt as they sweat, so they need it badly. Traders carried [[@salt|salt]] south on [[@camels|camels]] and took gold north to the Mediterranean. Mali's kings taxed this trade. Much of the gold used in Europe and North Africa at the time came from West Africa.

The [[empire|empire]] itself had been founded more than 70 years before Musa by Sundiata Keita, around the 1230s. His story is still sung by [[griot|griots]], the storytellers and musicians of West Africa.

Musa came back with scholars, judges and an architect, often named as Abu Ishaq al-Sahili. In Timbuktu he ordered the Djinguereber Mosque, built of mud brick and wood. A version of it still stands, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Over the next two centuries, Timbuktu became famous for learning. Students came to study religion, law, astronomy and mathematics. Families collected handwritten books, and hundreds of thousands of old [[manuscript|manuscripts]] survive in the region. In 2012 and 2013, during fighting in northern Mali, librarians quietly smuggled many of them to safety.

About 15 years after Musa died, the Moroccan traveller [[@ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]] visited Mali during the reign of Musa's brother, Mansa Sulayman. He praised how safe the roads were and wrote that travellers did not fear thieves. He also grumbled about the gifts he received, which he thought were too small.

Mali's fame reached Europe. On the Catalan Atlas, made in Majorca in 1375, Mansa Musa sits on a throne wearing a gold crown. He holds a gold nugget up to a rider approaching on a camel. For European mapmakers who had never been to Africa, Mali meant one thing: gold.

The empire weakened in the 1400s, and the Songhai Empire took over much of its land. Today, Mansa Musa often appears on lists of the richest people in history. Those lists use guesswork, and the comparisons don't really work. What we do know is that a West African king once caught the attention of half the known world.

text: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are a chain of about 836 islands and islets in the Bay of Bengal. Only a few dozen have people living on them. The Andamans lie to the north and the Nicobars to the south. Together they form a union [[territory|territory]] of India, though they are far closer to Myanmar, [[@thailand|Thailand]] and Indonesia than to Chennai.

The islands are special for their [[@coral-bleaching|coral reefs]] and rainforests, for some of the oldest human communities in the world, and for a painful place in India's freedom struggle. Visitors come for white beaches such as Radhanagar, on Swaraj Dweep, and for clear water full of fish.

st.prompt: India has only one confirmed active volcano. Where is it?

options.t: Barren Island, in the Andaman Sea
In the Western Ghats, near Goa

st.reveal: Barren Island lies about 140 km north-east of the Andamans' capital. It has erupted many times since the 1990s. Nobody lives there, although goats left by sailors long ago have survived on the island.

src: Andaman and Nicobar Administration, Government of India, about the islands.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

d.try: Make a mini reef map. On a sheet of paper, draw an island and a ring of coral around it in the shallow sea. Use a blue pencil for deep water and light blue for shallow. Add the animals you'd find at each depth, using a book or the Kyun app. Coral needs sunlight, so it only grows in the light blue zone.
myth: The Andaman Islands lie just off the coast of India.
They are about 1,200 km from Chennai and Kolkata, across the Bay of Bengal. The southern tip of the Nicobar Islands is only about 150 km from Indonesia's Sumatra.

sec.t:
People have lived on the islands for many thousands of years. Several of their oldest communities are still there. The Great Andamanese, Jarawa, Onge and Sentinelese live in the Andamans, and the Shompen and Nicobarese in the Nicobars.

The Sentinelese live on North Sentinel Island and make it clear that they do not want visitors. Indian law forbids anyone from going near the island. This protects them from diseases they have no defence against and lets them live their own way. Some of the other groups are now very small in number, and India tries to protect their forests and way of life.

The British built a large prison at Port Blair, the old capital, now called Sri Vijaya Puram. The Cellular Jail, completed in 1906, had 693 small cells, so each prisoner was kept alone. Many Indians who fought for freedom were sent there. People called the islands Kala Pani, "black water", because being sent across the sea meant being cut off from home and family.

The jail is now a national memorial. During the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], Japan occupied the islands, and in December 1943 [[@subhas-bose|Subhas Chandra Bose]] raised the Indian flag in Port Blair. Today the islands' story is an important part of India's [[@freedom-struggle|freedom struggle]].

The islands sit near the edge of two plates of Earth's crust. Barren Island, about 140 km from the capital, is India's only confirmed active [[@volcano|volcano]]. It has erupted many times since 1991.

On 26 December 2004, a huge earthquake off Sumatra caused a [[@tsunami|tsunami]]. The Nicobar Islands were hit very hard, and many people died. Reports said some [[indigenous|indigenous]] communities, such as the Onge, survived by moving to high ground after noticing changes in the sea, using knowledge passed down through generations.

In 2018, three islands were renamed: Ross Island became Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Dweep, Neil Island became Shaheed Dweep, and Havelock became Swaraj Dweep. In 2024 Port Blair was renamed Sri Vijaya Puram. Some people welcomed the new names as a way to honour India's freedom fighters. Others were used to the old ones, which had been in use for well over a century. Either way, getting there still takes a two-hour flight or a ship journey of about three days from the mainland.

text: Gol Gumbaz is a giant tomb in Vijayapura, in northern [[@karnataka|Karnataka]], finished around 1656 for Sultan Mohammed Adil Shah. Its dome is about 44 metres across on the outside, one of the largest built anywhere before modern steel and concrete.

The dome echoes because sound bounces off its hard, curved inside again and again. A clap travels up, hits the dome, comes back down, bounces off the floor and goes up again. Each round trip takes a fraction of a second, so you hear the clap repeat several times before it fades. Guides often say seven. Around the base of the dome runs a balcony called the whispering gallery, where even a soft whisper travels round the curved wall to the far side.

st.prompt: In the whispering gallery, why can a whisper be heard clearly on the far side of the dome?

options.t: The sound hugs the curved wall and bounces all the way round
There are hidden pipes inside the walls
The dome makes sounds louder by itself

st.reveal: Sound waves hitting a curved wall at a shallow angle keep bouncing along it, like a marble rolling round the inside of a bowl. Little energy is lost, so the whisper arrives on the other side still clear.

src: Archaeological Survey of India, Gol Gumbaz, Bijapur.
Britannica, Gol Gumbaz.
Karnataka Tourism, Government of Karnataka, Vijayapura.
n.certNote: The echoes and the whispering gallery are real and easy to hear. The exact number of echoes depends on how loud the sound is and how noisy the hall is, so the famous "seven times" is a rough count, not a fixed rule.

d.try: Stand near a long, smooth wall or the corner of a big empty hall with a friend at the other end. Each of you put your face close to the wall and whisper. Then try it standing away from the wall. Notice how much clearer the sound is when it can travel along the surface.
myth: The echo in Gol Gumbaz was made by a hidden trick or machine.
There is no trick. The echoes come from the shape of the dome and its smooth, hard plaster, which reflect sound many times before it fades. Any similar dome would echo too.

sec.t:
The Adil Shahi sultans ruled Bijapur, in the Deccan, from the late 1400s to 1686. They were great builders. Mohammed Adil Shah began his own tomb early in his reign, and it took about 30 years to finish.

The building is a huge cube with a seven-storey tower at each corner, each topped with a small dome. Above sits the main dome. The single hall inside covers about 1,700 square metres, bigger than six tennis courts, with no pillars at all. The sultan's grave lies in the middle.

sec.h: How do you hold up a dome without pillars?
sec.t:
A round dome doesn't sit easily on a square room. The builders solved this with arches across the corners that turn the square into an eight-sided shape, then into a circle. These overlapping arches spread the dome's huge weight down into the thick walls.

The dome is made of bricks and lime mortar, a few metres thick. It is a little like the domes of cathedrals in Europe, where builders used similar tricks. Some people say Gol Gumbaz's dome is second in size only to St Peter's in Rome among old domes, though such rankings depend on how you measure.

Visitors climb a long, narrow staircase inside one of the corner towers to reach the gallery. It is a narrow balcony that runs right round the base of the dome, about 33 metres above the floor.

If you whisper close to the wall, the sound clings to the curved surface and bounces along it all the way round. A friend on the opposite side, about 37 metres away, can hear you clearly. Many visitors clap and shout too, which is why the gallery is rarely quiet.

Gol Gumbaz is not alone. St Paul's Cathedral in London has a famous whispering gallery, and in the 1870s the British scientist Lord Rayleigh studied it to explain how such waves work. In New York, a curved tiled arch in Grand Central Terminal lets two people whisper to each other from opposite corners.

Builders who want quiet rooms do the opposite. They use soft, rough or angled surfaces that stop sound from bouncing. And the strangest part? Recording studios spend a lot of money to stop exactly the echoes that make Gol Gumbaz famous, using [[@soundproofing|soundproofing]] tricks.

text: Braille is a code of raised dots that you read by touch. Each letter sits in a small space called a cell, which has room for six dots in two columns of three. Different patterns of raised dots stand for different letters, numbers and [[@words-punctuation|punctuation marks]]. One dot in the top left is "a". Two dots down the left side are "b".

A trained reader slides the fingertips lightly along a line, feeling each pattern as a whole rather than counting dots. Fingertips are packed with touch [[sensor|sensors]] in the [[@skin|skin]], and experienced readers move along a line surprisingly quickly.
Louis Braille, a blind French student, created the system as a teenager in 1824.

st.prompt: How many dot positions are there in one braille cell?
st.reveal: A braille cell has six positions, two columns of three, small enough to fit under one fingertip. Charles Barbier's earlier "night writing" used up to twelve dots, which was too big to feel in one touch.

src: Royal National Institute of Blind People (RNIB), history of braille.
American Foundation for the Blind, Louis Braille and the braille system.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Louis Braille.

d.try: Draw a grid of two columns and three rows on paper, about the size of a fingertip, then make a bigger copy. Use dried beans or buttons to "raise" dots and build the braille letters a to e from a braille chart. Close your eyes and ask someone to make a letter for you to read by touch.
myth: Braille is a language.
Braille is a code for writing languages, not a language itself. The same six-dot cells are used to write English, French, Hindi, Tamil and many others.

sec.t:
Louis Braille was born in 1809 in Coupvray, a village east of Paris. At the age of three, playing in his father's leather workshop, he hurt one eye with a sharp tool. [[infection|Infection]] spread to both eyes, and by five he was completely blind.

At ten he won a place at the Royal Institute for Blind Youth in Paris. Its books were printed in large raised letters, pressed into heavy paper. They were enormous, expensive and slow to read, because fingers struggle to tell curvy letters like O and Q apart. The school owned only a small number of them.

Six dots, each either raised or flat, give 64 combinations. Leave out the blank cell, and 63 patterns remain. That's enough for the alphabet, numbers, punctuation and many common short words. It's the same counting trick a computer uses with its 0s and 1s, which is why braille is sometimes compared to [[@binary-code|binary code]].

Braille has been adapted to many languages. Bharati Braille uses shared patterns for similar sounds across [[@hindi-language|Hindi]], Tamil, Bengali and other Indian languages, so a reader who knows one can learn the others more easily. Refreshable braille displays, with tiny pins that pop up and down, let blind people read emails and websites. Like [[@sign-language|sign language]] for deaf people, braille opened up schools, jobs and libraries.

Braille's own school did not officially adopt his system until 1854, two years after he died of [[@tb-india|tuberculosis]] at the age of 43. Some sighted teachers had preferred raised print, which they could read themselves. The students kept using his dots anyway.

Today braille appears on lift buttons, on medicine boxes in Europe, and on signs at railway stations and airports, and many countries have laws about [[@disabilities-inclusion|access for disabled people]]. In 1952, a hundred years after his death, Louis Braille's remains were moved to the Panthéon in Paris, where France honours its national heroes. Every 4 January, his birthday, World Braille Day remembers the boy who made books fit under a fingertip.

text: Most food makes a long trip. A farmer grows and harvests it. It is packed and carried, by bullock cart, tractor, truck, train or ship, to a market. Traders buy it there in bulk and sell it on to shops, restaurants and street vendors. Finally someone buys it, carries it home and cooks it.
Along the way, food has to be kept clean and cool, and every person in the chain takes a small share of the price. Some foods travel a few kilometres. Others cross oceans.

st.prompt: Which of these usually travels the farthest to reach a supermarket in the United States?
st.reveal: Bananas grow in warm, wet places, and most sold in the US come from countries such as Guatemala and Ecuador. They travel thousands of kilometres by ship in chilled containers. Milk and bread are usually made much closer to where they are sold.

src: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), food supply chains.

d.try: Look at the stickers on fruit and the labels on packets in your kitchen. Write down every place or country you find. Mark them on a map or a globe and see which food travelled the farthest.
myth: Food grown nearby is always better for the planet.

For most foods, transport is only a small part of their climate impact. How the food is grown, and what kind of food it is, usually matters much more. Local food can still be fresher and support nearby farmers.
facts: keeping food chilled from farm to shop
Biggest share of food's climate impact

sec.t:
In India, many farmers sell their crops at a mandi, a regulated wholesale market. [[@delhi|Delhi]]'s Azadpur Mandi is one of the largest fruit and vegetable markets in Asia. Before sunrise, trucks arrive loaded with onions from Maharashtra, [[@apples|apples]] from [[@himachal|Himachal Pradesh]] and potatoes from Uttar Pradesh.

Commission agents and traders bid for the produce. It is then sold to smaller traders, who supply local markets, carts and [[@shops-markets|shops]]. By breakfast time, vegetables picked the day before can be on a sabziwala's cart in your street.

In the United States, many farms are very large and grow just one or two crops. Food often goes from the farm to a packing plant, then to a huge distribution warehouse, then by truck to supermarkets. California grows a large share of the country's fruit and vegetables, so lettuce may cross the whole continent to reach New York.

Some food travels even farther. Most [[@bananas|bananas]] eaten in the US come from Central and South America, carried in refrigerated ships.

When you pay for a kilo of onions, the money is shared out. The farmer gets a part, and so do the transporter, the trader, the market and the shop. Farmers often receive much less than half of the final price, though this varies a lot by crop and place.

That is why some farmers now sell directly, through farmers' markets in American towns or farmer producer groups and apps in India. Cutting out steps can mean fresher food and a fairer share.

Food is often changed a little before it travels. Wheat is milled into atta, milk is [[pasteurise|pasteurised]] and packed, and peas are [[@frozen-food|frozen within hours of picking]]. Some fruit is picked before it is fully ripe so it does not get squashed on the way.

[[@food-why-bananas-curve|Bananas]] are a good example. They are picked green and shipped cold, then ripened in special rooms filled with a natural plant gas called ethylene. Mangoes in Indian markets are sometimes ripened in warm piles of straw. Each step is a small race against time and [[microbe|microbes]].

Many people think the best food is always local. Researchers at Our World in Data found that, for most foods, transport makes up only a small part of their [[climate|climate]] impact. Shipping is fairly efficient. What matters more is how the food is produced, and especially whether it is meat, dairy or plants. The exception is food sent by air, like some fresh berries, which has a much larger footprint per kilo.

text: About a fifth of the world's people eat with chopsticks, mostly in China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam. They began in China more than 3,000 years ago, first as cooking tools for stirring pots and fishing food out of boiling water.

Over time they became eating tools too. Many East Asian dishes are cut into small pieces in the kitchen, so diners don't need knives at the table. Noodles, dumplings, rice and small bits of vegetables and meat are easy to pick up with two sticks. And once chopsticks became part of good manners, people kept using them for everything.

st.prompt: In Japan, why are chopsticks usually shorter and more pointed than in China?

options.t: Japanese meals include lots of fish, and pointed tips help pick out bones
A law sets the length of chopsticks

st.reveal: Fish is central to Japanese cooking, and pointed tips are handy for separating flesh from bones. Meals are usually served in individual portions, so you don't need long chopsticks to reach shared dishes in the middle of the table.

src.Q. Edward Wang, Chopsticks: A Cultural and Culinary History (Cambridge University Press, 2015).

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, chopsticks.
n.certNote: The history of chopsticks is well studied, but why they spread is partly explained by theories, such as fuel shortages and Confucian ideas, that historians still discuss.

sec.t:
One popular idea is about fuel. Wood for cooking fires was scarce in parts of ancient China, so cooks chopped food small to cook it quickly. Small pieces suit chopsticks.

Another idea links them to [[@confucius|Confucius]], the teacher whose ideas shaped Chinese manners. A saying linked to his followers suggests that a gentleman keeps knives, tools of the slaughterhouse, away from the table. Historians aren't sure how much this mattered, but it shows how eating tools were tied to ideas of politeness.

Chopsticks spread from China to Vietnam, Korea and Japan, and each changed them. Chinese chopsticks are long, often around 25 cm, with blunt ends, good for reaching dishes shared in the middle of the table. Japanese hashi are shorter and pointed. Korean chopsticks are usually flat and made of stainless steel, and Koreans eat rice and soup with a spoon.

Vietnamese chopsticks are long like Chinese ones. Thailand is the surprise. People there mostly eat with a fork and spoon, keeping chopsticks for noodles.

Chopsticks are a clever piece of physics. The bottom stick stays still, resting against your fingers. The top stick pivots near your thumb like a pair of pincers. That makes chopsticks a kind of [[@lever-lift|lever]], turning a small movement of your fingertips into a precise pinch at the far end.

Skilled users can pick up a single grain of rice or a slippery peanut. Some studies suggest that children who learn chopsticks early develop good finger control, though it is hard to prove.

Chopsticks come with rules. In Japan and China, sticking them upright in a bowl of rice looks like the incense sticks placed at funerals, so it's considered very rude. In Japan, passing food from one pair of chopsticks to another is avoided because it echoes a funeral [[ritual|ritual]]. Pointing or waving with chopsticks is impolite almost everywhere.

Disposable wooden chopsticks are a modern problem. China alone is estimated to use tens of billions of pairs a year, which means cutting down many trees. Some people now carry their own reusable pair.

In India, chopsticks arrived with Chinese migrants in Kolkata and later spread with the craze for [[@chinese-food-india|Indo-Chinese food]]. Many Indians happily eat hakka noodles with chopsticks and dal-chawal with their fingers. That second habit has science of its own, explored in [[@food-eating-with-hands|eating with your hands]].
